newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang says he sees no conflict with U.S..
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang says he sees no conflict with U.S..

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Friday said he did not think China and the United States were headed for conflict as Beijing had no territorial ambitions and was a champion of peace.
"I don't believe that China and the United States are going to have a conflict," Jiang said in an interview with Cable News Network (CNN).
"The Chinese government and people love peace," Jiang said, adding worries that Beijing could become a threat to world peace were the result of Cold War thinking.
"China has never had the intention for expansion," Jiang said.
Sino-U.S. ties plunged after Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui made a landmark, private trip to the United States in June 1995.
China ruffled feathers in the region when it conducted war games and missiles tests near arch rival Taiwan in the run-up to presidential elections on the island in March 1996.
Ties with the United States were further strained when Washington backed Taiwan by sending aircraft carriers to waters near the island during the war games.

Relations have also been troubled by feuding over issues such as human rights and weapons proliferation, but have warmed in recent months as both sides have laboured to keep the cross-Pacific relationship on track.
Jiang said a state visit to the United States scheduled for later this year would allow him to touch base with President Bill Clinton and other U.S. leaders.
"To exchange visits... will surely contribute to our joint efforts to establish a healthy and stable Sino-U.S. relationship oriented towards the 21st Century," he said.

But Jiang sounded a note of warning to Washington over Taiwan -- split from the mainland since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949 -- saying the issue was the most sensitive point in the bumpy relationship.
"If the Taiwan question is not handled properly, Sino-U.S. relations will experience twists and turns, and it will be difficult to enjoy healthy and stable growth," Jiang said.
China could learn from the United States in terms of science and economic management, Jiang said, but he indicated Beijing would not adopt American-style democracy or Western views on human rights.
"It's impossible for all the countries in the world to have entirely the same social systems and democratic practices."

China has come under heavy fire from the United States and other Western nations for its heavy-handed treatment of political dissent. Beijing has dismissed such criticism as interference in it internal affairs.
